subject: Copywriting
title: Rosser Reeves: The Unique Selling Proposition
description: One-minute skill: Rosser Reeves: The Unique Selling Proposition.

hook.text: 'Melts in your mouth, not in your hands.' Rosser Reeves wrote that line for M&Ms. It's one clear promise—his method.

buildup.text: Reeves created the Unique Selling Proposition: every ad must propose one specific benefit no competitor offers.

discovery.text: He demanded repetition. The same ad, unchanged, running until the numbers declined. Creativity was secondary to results.

twist.text: The creative revolution hated Reeves. They called him formulaic. But his ads outsold theirs by every measurable metric.

climax.text: His USP concept still drives branding today.

punchline.text: One proposition. Relentlessly repeated. The USP still wins.

details.summary: Rosser Reeves of Ted Bates & Company invented the Unique Selling Proposition, arguing every ad must make a specific promise no competitor offers. His USP framework — behind M&M's 'Melts in Your Mouth, Not in Your Hands' — became one of advertising's most enduring strategic tools.
details.whyItMatters: The USP framework gives every brand a clear, defensible position. Without it, messages become generic and forgettable. It remains the starting point for most brand positioning exercises.
takeaways: Every ad must propose a unique benefit the competition cannot claim
The M&M's slogan is a perfect example of the USP in action
Reeves prioritized repetition and consistency over creative variety

faq.question: What exactly is a Unique Selling Proposition?
faq.answer: A USP has three requirements: it must make a specific proposition to the customer, the proposition must be one that competitors either cannot or do not offer, and it must be strong enough to pull new customers to the product.

faq.question: Is the USP concept still relevant in modern marketing?
faq.answer: Absolutely. While markets are more crowded, the need for differentiation is greater than ever. Every strong brand strategy starts by identifying what makes the offering unique. The language has evolved to 'positioning' and 'value proposition,' but the core idea is Reeves's USP.
